query:
The family operates with an understanding that when Nkechi cooks for a gathering, everyone eats what she has prepared without requesting alternatives. Does this expectation apply to all family members equally? If not, who behaves differently, and what makes this visible without it becoming a conflict?

Options:
A. Emeka
B. Tobenna
C. Ifeoma
D. Chisom
context:
[1] (about=Nkechi, episodic, t14 @2025-12-07T18:11:00) My children. I will make egusi with stockfish. Ifeoma, I have remembered every year but it is good that you mentioned it. The menu is settled then: ofe onugbu, jollof, egusi with stockfish. Kingsley handles his suya outside. Adaeze brings chin chin and puff puff. 🙏

agent_answer:
Not equally. The person who behaves differently is **Kingsley** — none of the listed options (Emeka, Tobenna, Ifeoma, Chisom).

Kingsley says he is bringing suya, will handle the meat, and “nobody is eating dry chicken” while he’s there; he even offers to bring his own grill. That departs from the expectation that everyone eats what Nkechi has prepared. It stays non-conflictual because Nkechi sets a boundary — “the kitchen in this house is not a barbecue pit” — but allows it if the smoke stays outside, and later folds it into the settled menu as “Kingsley handles his suya outside.”

Emeka has no relevant food-alternative record; Tobenna and Chisom have no record; Ifeoma’s mention of egusi with stockfish is not an alternative request — Nkechi says she “remembered every year” and already prepares it.
